extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, correspondents, copy-readers, and copy editors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and handling rules for preparing, submitting, and punctuating newspaper copy (how to write/type/arrange pages and specific punctuation/capitalization/orthography conventions used in newsrooms).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Typewriter
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requirement in preparing copy is a knowledge of how to handle a typewriter dexterously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are furnished with typewriters; longhand copy rarely is sent to compositors. If longhand arrives it is usually typed by stenographers or reporters before dispatch to the composing room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longhand Copy
rubrics_metrics.description: When away from the office and forced to write longhand, write with painstaking care for accuracy; legible copy survives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print unusual proper names and technical words letter by letter; underscore/overscore letters likely to be confused (underscore u and a, overscore n and o); use half-circle marks for quotation marks to show beginning or end; use a small cross or circled period instead of a plain period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Use office-supplied writing paper if provided; if not, choose unglazed paper of a neutral tint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended sizes: unruled print paper 6x9 or 8½x11 inches, of sufficient firmness for ink or pencil; include self-addressed envelopes when supplied by the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave the top half of the first page blank (except writer's name in a ring at extreme left); all sheets should have one-inch margins on sides and bottom; non-first sheets should have an inch top margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Side margins allow corrections by copy editors, bottom margins allow pasting sheets together, top margins are necessary for paging and headline writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph Indention
rubrics_metrics.description: All paragraphs, including the first, should be indented an inch and marked with the paragraph sign (a rectangle) placed before the first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two paragraphs have been run together, insert paragraph sign immediately before new paragraph and repeat in the margin; put paragraph sign at end of page if paragraph completes the page so compositor knows not to conclude with broken line; only first lines of paragraphs (except quotations and summaries) should be indented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: When consolidating separately written paragraphs, mark the change so compositors know the matter is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw a line from the end of the first to the beginning of the second and mark 'No 1' in the margin; use similar marks when lines/sentences canceled should be continuous. Use diagonal lines across page breaks to indicate a paragraph continues on next sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowded Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not crowd lines together; when typewritten, set triple spacing; when longhand, leave quarter-inch between lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowded lines cause extra work for copy-readers; exception only when a paragraph is a trifle too long for a page—better to crowd last lines slightly than run words to next page.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pages (one side only and numbering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write on more than one side of a sheet; number pages at top with arabic numerals enclosed in a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paragraph would normally begin on the last line of a page, leave the line blank and start the paragraph on a fresh sheet. Big dailies cut sheets into 'takes' sent to different compositors—writing on both sides causes confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make as few corrections as possible; for considerable additions, cut the page and paste in the addition rather than write in the margin or on a separate sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fold the lower edge forward to match length of other sheets; do not fold backward (folds may be unnoticed and cause confusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Add Stories" and Add/Insert Marking
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is incomplete or additional material follows, mark 'More' in a circle at foot of page or use 'Add' and 'Insert' slugs enclosed in rings with clear catch lines and addition numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Add 1, Saloon Robbery'; inserts slugged 'Insert A, Saloon Robbery' with precise place indicated at top of inserted page: 'Insert after first paragraph of lead, Saloon Robbery.' Rings prevent compositors from setting the directions in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations and Clippings
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate approximate placement of cuts/illustrations by 'Turn rule for cut' and paste clippings into the copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make-up editor may change position for balance, but marking aids accurate placement; pins and clips slip easily and may cause loss—paste clippings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underscoring for Type Indication
rubrics_metrics.description: Underscore once for italics, twice for SMALL CAPITALS, three times for CAPITALS; use wave-line underscoring for display type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many newspapers no longer use italics/small caps due to linotype limitations—where emphasis was formerly by underscoring, reword the sentence instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections (marking deletions and changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Run pen/pencil through letters or words to be struck out and draw a line between words to be set up together; do not enclose deletions in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wrongly struck out, restore by a series of dots beneath and write 'stet' in margin. Indicate transposition by drawing a continuous line over first and under second and write 'tr' in margin. Indicate a capital that should be small by drawing a line downward from right to left through the letter. Circle abbreviations/figures/ampersands to be spelled out; do not 'ring' without certainty. For slang/misspelled/ungrammatical copy to be set as written, put 'Follow Copy' in the margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: The End (end mark and final handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark completion of the story with an end mark (#) or figure 10 in a circle (telegrapher's sign); read every page carefully correcting all errors and give it to city editor unfolded if possible, never rolled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inconvenient to keep pages flat, fold lengthwise (not crosswise); sheets should not be pinned together—the pin betrays novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story in Type (proofreading and learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter should read his story carefully after it has appeared in print to detect errors and note changes made at city desk to learn what is expected and improve style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping carbon copies and comparing them word for word with printed articles helps a writer change his style for the better.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Rules of Punctuation (importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every well-regulated newspaper has its own punctuation rules, but reporters should know general rules of punctuation because bad punctuation is worse than bad spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough knowledge of the following rules of punctuation is practically a necessity for successful journalistic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Proper Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all proper names (designating particular person, place, or thing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general principle to apply across specific subcases below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Titles of Books, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word and all important words in titles of books, newspapers, magazines, articles, poems, plays, pictures, etc.; do not capitalize articles, demonstratives, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs, relative pronouns, and other pronouns in possessive case unless first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preceding 'The' to a newspaper or magazine title is regarded as part of the title and is capitalized. Example: Two copies of The Atlanta Constitution were produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Names and Titles of the Deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and titles of the Deity and of Jesus Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Names of the Bible and Sacred Books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of the Bible and other sacred books, versions, and books/divisions of the Bible; do not capitalize adjectives derived from such names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right: The Koran, the Septuagint, the Old Testament, Psalms; but biblical, scriptural, apocryphal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Titles of Respect, Honor, Office, Profession
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize such titles when they immediately precede proper names; do not capitalize them elsewhere in the sentence. The prefix 'ex-' before a title is not capitalized and does not affect capitalization of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right: The Rev. Samuel Plantz, President Wilson, ex-President Roosevelt, Senator Newlands. Not capitalized when following name: the archbishop and the senator were in conference with Mr. Bryan, former secretary of state under President Wilson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Names Indicating Nationality or Locality
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names distinguishing nationality or locality (e.g., Yankee, Creole, Hoosier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Names of Athletic Teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of athletic teams (e.g., Giants, Cubs, Badgers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Festivals and Holidays
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin names of festivals and holidays with capital letters (e.g., Easter, Thanksgiving, Labor day).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Societies, Political Parties, Organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of clubs, secret societies, religious denominations, colleges, political parties, corporations, railroads, and organizations generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Riverview Country club, Elks, Baptist church, Mills college, Republican party, Santa Fe railroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Ordinal Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ordinal numbers denoting sessions of congress, political divisions, and city wards with capital letters (e.g., Sixty-second congress, Third ward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Names of Buildings, Squares, Parks
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of buildings, blocks, squares, parks, drives, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Times building, Temple block, Yellowstone park, Sheridan road.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Common Nouns Joined with Proper Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize a common noun joined with a proper name when it precedes and means the same thing; do not capitalize the common noun if it follows the proper name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Columbia university, University of Chicago, First Presbyterian church, Church of the Savior, National Bank of North America, First National bank, Memorial day, Fourth of July.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Boards, Committees, Legislative Bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize names of boards, bureaus, offices, departments, committees, legal/legislative/political bodies when standing alone (e.g., school board, weather bureau).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: war office, health department, nominating committee, assembly, state senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Prefixes 'von', 'de', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize prefixes von, de, di, le, la, etc., except when they begin a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Capt. von Papen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Toasts
rubrics_metrics.description: In toasts, capitalize all the important words in the phrase indicating the person, place, or cause to which the toast is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'My Country — May it always be right; but, right or wrong, my country.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Nouns Followed by Numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize a noun followed by a numeral indicating position, place, or order of sequence (e.g., lot 14, block 3, act v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital Letters: Resolutions for Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions for debate, capitalize the 'Resolved' and the 'That' following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Resolved, That Missouri should establish schedules of minimum wages for workmen, constitutionality conceded.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Period: Roman Numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after roman numerals (e.g., Louis XIV of France).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Period: Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a period after abbreviated words and after single or double initial letters representing single words (e.g., Wm., Thos., Ph.D.).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Period: Contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put a period after contracted words, including nicknames (e.g., Bill, Tom, can't, hadn't).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Period: Side-Heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after side-heads, including figures at the beginning of a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the period after 'Side-Heads' at the beginning of the paragraph in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Colon: Formal Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to introduce a formal quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The author also makes this significant statement: 'There is every reason to believe that this disease plays a larger part...'

rubrics_metrics.name: The Colon: Formal Enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to introduce lists of the dead, injured, persons present, and similar enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Only four patrons appeared in this morning's police matinee: Chip Owens, Allie McGowan, Alfonso Bias, and Nick Muskowitz.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Colon: Time Indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a colon between hours and minutes, and minutes and seconds in time indications (e.g., 2:30, 1:42).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Colon: General Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon after any word, phrase, or clause when what follows explains or makes clear what precedes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Semicolon: Compound Sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to separate independent clauses in compound sentences that have no connective, though semicolon use is fast disappearing from newspaper columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage favors making a separate sentence of the second clause to avoid complex constructions. Examples provided with 'Better' and 'Permissible' variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Semicolon: Lists with Places
rubrics_metrics.description: In lists where the town or place of residence is given, separate different names by semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Allen Rogers of Los Vegas, N. M.; Orren Thomas of Benton, Mo.; Mr. and Mrs. Henry Barnes of Sioux City, la.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Semicolon: Athletic Results
rubrics_metrics.description: In athletic results, use a semicolon to separate team names and their scores (e.g., Cornell, 21; Syracuse, 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Semicolon: Instead of Commas
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon may be used instead of a comma when commas within a clause make relations unclear; use semicolon to keep larger phrase- and clause-relations clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Parenthetic Expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off parenthetic words, phrases, and clauses with commas when they cause marked interruption; if in doubt, omit the comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He, like many others, believes firmly in the Rightness of the new movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Words in Apposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off a word in apposition with another word that means the same thing by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Henry Owen, lineman for the local telegraph company, was the only witness of the accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: With 'namely', 'that is', etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma before and 'namely', 'viz.', 'that is', 'i.e.' when introducing an example, illustration, or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Contrasted Words and Phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off contrasted words and phrases with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hard work, not genius, was what enabled him to succeed. The faster they work, the better they are paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Introductory Words and Phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off introductory words, phrases, and clauses at the beginning of a sentence with commas when they modify the whole sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Yes, he had even tried to bribe the officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: In Direct Address
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off words used in direct address with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mark this, gentlemen of the jury, in his list of forgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Explanatory Dates and Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off a date explaining a previous date or a geographical name explaining a previous name with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: On April 2, 1916, she was arrested at Chicago, Ill.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Phrases Indicating Residence, Position, or Title
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma before 'of' in phrases indicating residence, position, or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Miss Helen Hahn of Gainesville, Mrs. Henry Bushman of Athens, Orren Cramer of Atlanta. Dwight O. Conklin of the Bessemer Smelting Company was the chief speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Academic and Honorary Titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off academic and honorary titles from proper names and from each other by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: President O. N. Fowler, Ph.D., LL.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Names Followed by Initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off baptismal names or initials following a surname by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Arendale, Charles V.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Words/Phrases/Clauses in a Series (Oxford comma guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate members of a series of words/phrases/clauses by commas; when series has three or more and conjunction used only before last two, the comma before conjunction may be omitted but better usage favors inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The teller was kicked, beaten, and robbed by four masked men.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: After Interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow slightly exclamatory interjections with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: 'oh' generally takes a comma after it (and is lowercase except at beginning), 'O' never; 'O' used in direct address. Examples: Ah, the happy days and the happy city! Oh, but the way the boys splashed!

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Short Quotations and Maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off short informal quotations and maxims with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He was last heard to say, 'If I don't return in time, call up the office.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: In Large Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas to separate large numbers into groups of three figures each; omit commas in dates and in street/telephone/automobile numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Athletic Scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma between the name of the team and its score in athletic scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New Orleans, 7; Memphis, 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Biblical Passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma between chapter and verse in citations of biblical passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: John 2, 15.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: Resolutions for Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions for debate, put a comma after 'Resolved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Resolved, That women should be given the right of suffrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comma: General Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to mark any distinct pause not indicated by other punctuation and to make clear any word/phrase/clause that may be obscure without a comma; omit commas except when distinctly necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: Sudden Break in Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash to mark a sudden suspension of the thought or a violent break in sentence construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'You mean to say — Just what are you talking about?'

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: Date Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a dash between the date or the Special and the beginning of the story in date-line stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sylvester, Ga., Jan. 21. — Five negroes were taken...

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: After 'namely', 'viz.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a dash after 'namely', 'as', 'that is', 'viz.', etc., when introducing an example or illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The mob seemed to hold him responsible for two things, namely — the lost key and the barred door.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: Lists of Officers
rubrics_metrics.description: In giving lists of officers, put a dash between the name of the office and the officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: President — O. N. Homer; Vice President — Abner King; Secretary — David Thoeder.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: Dialogue, Questions and Answers
rubrics_metrics.description: In quoting Q. and A. or dialogue, put a dash between the Q./A. or speaker's name and statement; make a new paragraph for each speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Q. — Are you a resident of Montana? A. — I have been for four years.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Dash: Slowness of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a dash between words or phrases to indicate slowness or hesitancy in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'These, he said, were his — er — wife's slippers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses: Political Parties and Identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: In legislative or congressional reports, enclose party, state, or county name in parentheses when giving political affiliation or origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. Smith (Dem., S. C.), Mr. Harris (Jefferson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses: General Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid parentheses within sentences; two short sentences are better than one long one containing a parenthetic expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence with a clause within parentheses can generally be cut into two sentences and made more effective for newspaper purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Direct Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation-marks to set off direct quotations printed in the same type/style as surrounding text; quotations within quotations use single marks, then double again for a third nested quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include end quotes; failure to include them is a common error causing annoyance to printers and proof-readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Quoted Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation includes more than one paragraph set in same type/style as context, put quotation-marks at beginning of each paragraph but omit at the end of every paragraph except the last; when set in smaller type, omit all quote marks at beginning and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule, quotations of more than one sentence are written in separate paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Quotations and Summaries (separate paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When alternately summarizing and quoting verbatim in reporting a speech or interview, do not include a direct quotation and a condensed summary in the same paragraph; make separate paragraphs for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text show quoted paragraphs separated from summarized narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Titles of Books, Plays, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose in quotation-marks the titles of books, dramas, songs, poems, stories, magazine articles, toasts, and lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Names of Newspapers, Vessels, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put titles/names of newspapers, magazines, paintings, vessels, cars, or animals in quotation-marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Slang and Technical Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose in quotation-marks slang and technical terms that are supposed to be unfamiliar to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-Marks: Nicknames
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put nicknames of persons or characters in plays/novels in quotation-marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ty Cobb, T. R., Heinle Zim, Becky Sharp.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Apostrophe: Possessive Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe and an 's' to indicate the singular possessive regardless of terminal s; use apostrophe and 's' for plural possessives not ending in s; use only apostrophe for plural possessives ending in s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Burns's house, Furness's hat; men's meeting, children's shoes; boys' hats, ladies' outfitter. For joint possessives put apostrophe after name nearest the thing possessed: Farmers and Merchants' bank, Allen and Bowen's Classical Mythology.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Apostrophe: Possessive Pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the apostrophe before the 's' in possessive pronouns (its, hers, theirs).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Apostrophe: Contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe in contracted words to indicate omitted letters (e.g., couldn't, he'll, you're).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Hyphen: Compound Words
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a hyphen between the members of a compound word; words compounded with specified prefixes/suffixes are generally hyphenated (list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of hyphenated compounds: able-bodied, attorney-general, basket-ball, brother-in-law, great-grandfather, post-mortem, quarter-back, shop-girl, to-day, to-morrow, to-night, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: Words Written Solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Words compounded with many common prefixes/suffixes are generally written solid; the guide provides a list of such prefixes/suffixes and example solid compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: anyone, baseball, football, newspaper, typewriter, schoolgirl, skyscraper, sidewalk, postmaster, tax-payer (taxpayer listed as 'taxpayer' in examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: Words Written Separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combinations should be written as two words (e.g., all right, any time, back yard, every time, fellow man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples list includes: all right, any time, back yard, half dollar, half dozen, mass meeting, pro tem, no one, some one (listed as 'some one').

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation: Compound Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound numbers between twenty and a hundred, when spelled out, should have a hyphen (e.g., twenty-one, forty-three).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Division Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing a word at the end of a line, observe rules: do not break a syllable awkwardly, don't divide monosyllables, don't separate consonant from vowel affecting pronunciation, don't divide diphthongs or separate two successive vowels where one is silent, don't separate a syllable added by an 's', don't divide hyphenated words except at regular hyphen, avoid awkward divisions, don't begin a line with a hyphen, generally avoid dividing words at line ends and never at end of page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of correct/incorrect divisions provided (cre-ditable vs cred-itable, noth-ing vs nothing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations: Avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations should as a rule be avoided; typewriter use has led to tendency to write out all words in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations: Personal and Professional Titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain personal and professional titles are abbreviated when preceding proper names (list provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Adjt. Gen., Brig. Gen., Capt., Col., Dr., Gen., Gov., Hon., Lieut., Maj., Mrs., Mr., Prof., Rev., Rt. Rev., Sergt., Supt., Mme., Mlle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use personal titles under specific restrictions (e.g., do not use 'Mr.' before a man's name when his baptismal name or initials are given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not Good example: 'Mr. A. B. Crayton of Belleville was a guest...' shows the rule in practice.
